title: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery
description: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.The 71-yea
body: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers.The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff. A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

schema.headline: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery

title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
description: Figure caption, Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on SaturdayByNick ThorpeCorrespondentReporting fromTirana, AlbaniaDemo
body: Figure caption, Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on SaturdayByNick ThorpeCorrespondentReporting fromTirana, AlbaniaDemonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row. Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests. The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard. Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days. Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic. Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyesBlack smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon. As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police. Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes. He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too."We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution. "Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."Image caption, Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana. She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights." She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.Image caption, Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades. The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030. He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity. Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule. Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni. She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest. Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups. Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions."Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC. "He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

schema.headline: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania

title: Swinney's emotional explanation for his commitment to independence
description: Figure caption, John Swinney said son is 'reason' for independenceByScotland political editorThis was a more emotional speech than we are used to from
body: Figure caption, John Swinney said son is 'reason' for independenceByScotland political editorThis was a more emotional speech than we are used to from John Swinney. His voice quivered as he explained that his personal commitment to the cause is for the future of his 15-year-old son, Matthew.Then the autocue stalled and the SNP leader is heard saying under his breath "oh, come on".A period of silence was broken by the conference crowd who came to his rescue with a standing ovation.Without the prime minister's name being mentioned, this section of the speech seemed to be a response to Andy Burnham's emotional appeal for the union in memory of his father at the Labour conference in Liverpool.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Andy Burnham has called for greater devolution in Scotland earlier this weekThere was a more obvious dig at the prime minister, who visited Motherwell this week to promote regional devolution within Scotland and drew on his experience as mayor of Greater Manchester.Again, without mentioning Andy Burnham by name, the first minister said: "Some think we should just be like Manchester. Well, I'm afraid I disagree."Scotland is no city. We are no region. We are a nation and soon we will be an independent nation."That went down well in the conference hall - even if the first minister is perfectly prepared to work with the prime minister on plans to create a regional level of government in Scotland, with powers transferred from both Westminster and Holyrood.Swinney also claimed that independence is "very close" in the full knowledge that there will not be another referendum unless there is a sustained surge in public support for Scottish statehood.Pledges on buses and misogynyPart of his strategy for achieving that is to demonstrate delivery in devolved government on issues of everyday concern.That's why he highlighted the roll out of the Scottish government's £2 bus fare cap as an example of cost of living support.It is already in place in the Highlands and across west central Scotland, and now he has confirmed its extension across north east Scotland from April.It should be available everywhere in Scotland by the end of this parliamentary term, by which time he said the Scottish government would, through franchising and regulation, have taken the bus network under public control.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, John Swinney, pictured with his son Matthew and wife, Elizabeth Quigley, at the SNP conference Announcements on making misogyny a specific criminal offence and new funding for community groups to fight racism are also designed to demonstrate a sense of immediate purpose.His speech seemed to energise those in the hall who are already with him. He also hopes it will engage those across Scotland who might be open to considering independence.Earlier this week, Swinney told me he is loving being first minister and intends to lead the SNP into the next Scottish Parliament election in 2031.However long he stays in office, this will always be a special conference for him - his first since leading his party through a successful Holyrood campaign and the one where he put the personal into his political commitment to independence.

schema.headline: Swinney's emotional explanation for his commitment to independence

title: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions
description: Figure caption, Watch: How does music on The Traitors manipulate your emotions?ByMusic correspondentSuspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman.
body: Figure caption, Watch: How does music on The Traitors manipulate your emotions?ByMusic correspondentSuspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman. The Traitors has it all.But the shadowiest of the show's shadowy secrets is its music.Have you ever noticed how the soundtrack manipulates your perception? A sinister orchestral flourish hints at a double cross. A cheeky chord injects humour into a kitchen conflab.As ever, though, you shouldn't trust what happens in the castle. The music can provide emphasis or act as misdirection, all at the producers' behest.Duplicity was baked into the music from the beginning."I remember the BBC was quite reluctant to even think about a show with murder as a main feature, so I knew I didn't want the music to go really dark," says Sam Watts, who composed the opening theme and much of the incidental score (but is not responsible for the show's haunting cover versions of well-known pop songs... more on those later).Watts, who had previously worked on Planet Earth and The Sarah Jane Adventures, pitched to work on the programme with only a basic idea of the set-up. It was only when he learned Winkleman was the host that he settled on his approach."They sent me a little shot they'd done of the opening with Claudia and the castle. That's when I knew it was going to be a bit camp and high drama and all the glorious things that Claudia brings to the show. So I just went with that - dark but fun."Image source, Sam WattsImage caption, Sam Watts' Traitors theme helped to establish the show's identityFor the title sequence, the 44-year-old wanted something memorable. As a kid, his favourite song was Bernard Hoffer's gloriously over-the-top Thundercats theme, external, so that's the level he aspired to."I was trying to write something that signified the show was starting, so that people would run in from making their cup of tea in the kitchen to watch it."And I wanted a memorable melody that people could hum, because it helps with the identity of the show."The Traitors theme is "one of the biggest pieces of music I've ever written", he says, recorded with a full orchestra and overdubbed with dozens of electronic elements to create a heightened, hyperreal atmosphere.That bled into the 20 or so other pieces Watts wrote, which also appear in dozens of international spin-offs.The idea, he says, is that the whole hour feels like a film trailer, with viewers permanently waiting for the psychological pressure chamber to explode.To achieve that, he employed several techniques of trailer music - most notably the "Braam", a klaxon-like punctuation mark invented for Christopher Nolan's Inception (see video for a fuller exploration).Show producer Sarah Fay took that concept and amplified it. "We wanted to just supersize it and make it feel like a drama, not like your usual reality [show]," she said in a rare interview with Metro, external when the first civilian series aired in 2022."We wanted to make it feel like that edge-of-your-seat cinematic drama with, you know, elements of Succession, and we wanted it to feel like Knives Out when you get into the castle!"To achieve that, she commissioned additional music from film trailer composers, including Hans Zimmer's company Bleeding Fingers. But she also sprinkled in a handful of creepy cover versions.Some became instant classics - such as a sinister spin on Britney Spears' Toxic, external, or a version of Tears For Fears' Mad World, external seemingly broadcast on a tannoy from Hades.They're so integral to The Traitors' aesthetic that it might surprise you to learn they weren't recorded specifically for the show.Image caption, The Traitors score has proved so popular that an entire BBC Proms concert was devoted to the show's music last yearBoth examples were created by German writer-producers 2wei.Based in Hamburg, they had no idea their music had appeared in The Traitors until friends in the UK messaged them in excitement."We were just flipping out," says 2wei's Simon Heeger. "It's completely different to how we ever thought it would be used."Heeger founded 2wei, pronounced "zwei", in 2016 with his old college friend Christian Vorländer.They had both spent time in LA working on advertisements and (stop me if you're sensing a theme here) film trailers, before moving home to build a music production empire."Christian worked on the Mad Max soundtrack, which is really known for the big drums and the orchestral scale – and that was really the starting point of our sound," says Heeger."Whenever you hear big epic drums with an orchestral sound and maybe a female vocal on top of it, it's usually something we had our fingers in."Image source, 2weiImage caption, Simon Heeger is the co-founder of 2wei, which is responsible for some of Traitors' most memorable cover songsTheir big break came with a stormy reworking of Destiny's Child's Survivor, which featured in the trailer to Alicia Vikander's Tomb Raider, external.Since then, their music has appeared in films like Wonder Woman and video games such as League of Legends. In The Traitors, original 2wei songs like Blindside, external now feature alongside their covers (other producers, including SYML and Damned Anthem also contribute songs to the show).Heeger says their background in commercials makes the music perfectly suited to the show's slippery skullduggery."In adverts, you only have a few seconds to convey a certain emotion and, especially in Traitors, where there are cliffhangers and moments that you don't expect, you need music that comes to the point right away but still has a boldness to it."It's a sweet spot, and it's not easy to convey, but every now and then it works quite well."Fans agree. On Spotify, there are hundreds of playlists dedicated to the programme's background music. Some are tailored to murder mystery parties and Halloween events. Others compile more sedate moments under labels like "gentle tension" or "chill elder emo watching Traitors".But never forget: the soundtrack is playing a deceitful game of its own."A lot of my music has a wink in it and, for The Traitors, it's a little silly and slightly over the top," says Watts."I think it helps the nastier side of things - the murder, the plotting - feel a bit more fun."

schema.headline: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions

title: Dubois vs Wardley 2: Londoner retains title with dominant second-round stoppage
description: Daniel Dubois underlined his status as Britain's leading heavyweight with a devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley to retain his WBO title
body: Daniel Dubois underlined his status as Britain's leading heavyweight with a devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley to retain his WBO title in London.The 29-year-old floored Wardley with a straight right inside the opening 20 seconds of their eagerly anticipated rematch at the O2 Arena and continued his relentless assault.Wardley survived the opening round but was overwhelmed by another sustained attack in the second, prompting his corner to throw in the towel.Dubois registers a second successive stoppage victory over Wardley, just five months after climbing off the canvas twice to dethrone his British rival in a thrilling 11-round contest in Manchester.This time, there was no such drama for the champion, who was dominant from the opening bell as he extended his professional record to 24 wins - 23 by knockout - and three defeats."Fabio is a great boy, coming in for the second time, but it was my time and my era. I had my intentions, bad intentions from the beginning," Dubois said. "My back was against the wall the first time, this time we just had to go out there and show that we mean business, which is what we did tonight."Wardley, 31, suffered the second defeat of his 23-fight professional career."I have always thrown myself in with the best competitors out there, the best in the business, the biggest, hardest, meanest guys around so, there is no shame in a loss when you're testing yourself against the best," he said.A sell-out crowd of 19,000 packed the O2 Arena and made their allegiances clear.Wardley's charismatic yet measured personality has made him a popular figure. He looked full of purpose as he took his time on stage, fireworks exploding in front of him, his usual smile replaced by a look of determination.Dubois, meanwhile, was greeted by jeers as he marched straight past the fireworks and towards the ring, wasting little time soaking up the occasion. Actor Paddy Considine, comedian Rob Beckett, Oasis star Noel Gallagher and darts world champion Luke Littler were among the famous faces in attendance.With 41 knockouts between the fighters, few expected the judges to be called upon. The feeling beforehand was that Wardley's best chance lay in making another fast start, having dropped Dubois inside the opening moments of their first meeting.But in a stunning reversal, it took just 17 seconds for Wardley to hit the canvas as Dubois backed him into a corner and landed a straight right.Chants of 'oh Fabio Wardley' were quickly silenced as Dubois continued to unload punishing combinations. Another furious attack towards the end of the round left Wardley in deep trouble.Trainer Ben Davison, criticised for not withdrawing Wardley sooner in their first contest, stood poised with a towel in his hand as his fighter survived to the bell. There had already been concerns over whether Wardley had returned too quickly after the punishment he absorbed in May, when he was left bloodied and badly swollen.And those fears appeared justified as the challenger struggled to cope with Dubois' relentless pressure. Wardley's hands were low and his punches wild and telegraphed, lacking the menace he had shown in Manchester.Backed into the corner again in the second round, he was subjected to another barrage before Davison leapt up and threw in the towel.Dubois continues to fly the flag for British heavyweight boxing. After losing to Oleksandr Usyk in 2023, he responded with impressive victories over Jarrell Miller, Filip Hrgovic and Anthony Joshua, only to suffer another defeat by Usyk last year.But back-to-back stoppage victories over Wardley have reinforced his standing among the world's leading active heavyweights.IBF champion Hrgovic, whom Dubois stopped in June 2024, entered the ring afterwards, with both men keen on a rematch.However, promoter Frank Warren wants Hrgovic to make his first title defence in Croatia before pursuing a unification fight.The biggest payday for Dubois could come against the winner of Joshua and Tyson Fury's December showdown, which is expected to have the WBA 'super' title at stake.Asked who he wants to face next, Dubois said: "Whoever is next in line, really. I'm the champion now, and I want to get some big fights in. At this stage in my career, big money, big fights."For Wardley, successive defeats represent a significant setback, but his remarkable journey should not be forgotten.The former recruitment consultant had just four white-collar fights before turning professional in 2017. Less than a decade later, he was a world heavyweight champion.Rather than rebuild against lesser opposition following May's punishing defeat, Wardley gambled on an immediate rematch with one of the division's most destructive punchers.It was a gamble that backfired and, after two bruising defeats, he may benefit from some time away.

schema.headline: Dubois vs Wardley 2: Londoner retains title with dominant second-round stoppage

title: Manifest: From reality TV to Wembley arena in one turbulent year
description: A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the follo
body: A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the following night.As the staging - complete with giant LED screens and the group's logo - is set up around them, the six members rehearse synchronised choreography alongside their back-up dancers.The group consists of main vocalist Sueda Uluca, lead vocalist Lidya Pınar, sub-vocalist Mina Solak, sub-vocalist and main rapper Zeynep Sude Oktay, lead dancer Hilal Yelekçi and main dancer Esin Bahat.But Wembley is just the beginning of their ambitions."After Wembley, we'll manifest Coachella and other big stages," says Hilal Yelekçi, playing on the group's name.manifest were formed in February last year through the Turkish reality TV talent competition Big5 Türkiye, which saw contestants compete over several months for a place in the group.They were mentored by established Turkish pop stars, including Gülçin Ergül, a former member of girl group Hepsi, who was also a judge on the show.The band's rise has been rapid, and they now have more than six million monthly listeners on Spotify.While in London, they released their first English-language single, TRALALA, which topped YouTube's daily music video chart on its release, ahead of videos from Shakira and Taylor Swift.The music video was also their first to be filmed outside Turkey, with the group working with a largely British production crew in east London."Getting out from that safe zone was a bit stressful for us," says Pınar.Despite their hopes to perform on British and American stages, they're keen to retain their Turkish identity."We want to reach a global audience with our Turkish songs actually, not with English ones," says Sude Oktay."We want to teach people to sing in Turkish."Alongside Turkish girl group Hepsi, manifest cite the Spice Girls among their musical inspirations.Pınar says her favourite Spice Girl is Baby Spice."Because of the pink. I'm pink and blonde, so it's obvious," she laughs.They have also had the chance to meet one of the world's biggest pop stars, Dua Lipa. The British-Albanian singer met manifest backstage before watching them perform at her Sunny Hill Festival in Kosovo in July this year."She came to our backstage and said a lot of great things," one member recalls."We really love her, her songs, her stage presence."On the day of the concert, there was a sense of excitement outside Wembley Arena as fans wearing manifest-branded headbands and carrying banners gathered.The crowd was predominantly Turkish women in their 20s and 30s, many dressed in colours associated with the group. Among them were friends Elif, 31, and Zeynep, 25, both Turkish women living in London, who reflected on the band's past year."I don't think I've ever heard of a girl band performing there," says Zeynep."I think I was seven when Hepsi were last together. It's maybe a once-in-a-lifetime experience."Turkish pop star Tarkan previously performed at Wembley Arena in 2008.For Elif, the concert has a wider significance."We are going through difficult times back home. It means girl power and empowerment, and just having fun and being together," she says."I feel like back home people came together to support them and criticise the treatment that they were receiving from the government."Zeynep hopes the group will one day be able to perform freely in Turkey."It's great to see them here, but I hope one day they will be back in Turkey and they'll be able to do whatever they want without getting persecuted for it," she says.

schema.headline: Manifest: From reality TV to Wembley arena in one turbulent year

title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
description: US President Donald Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart V
body: US President Donald Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the president in September. But Trump issued an executive order Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the suspension would consist of a 60-day pause intended  to analyse the impact on the global economy.The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy by giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.Rubio said Trump wanted to use the 60 days to analyse "what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy".Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.Since then, Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.The sanctions suspension seemed to add further fuel to the fire, while Russia welcomed it.Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Trump's order was "an important and truly historic moment".Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage", primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations.Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X. A handful of Republicans, too, came out against the move.Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a Trump ally, called waiving the sanctions a mistake, saying on Fox News: "I wish the president hadn't done it."He added there were other ways to address diesel prices and "the current path, unfortunately, just... benefits Putin and that's not a good idea."Senator John Cornyn, also of Texas, said on X: "Helping Putin in Ukraine is reckless. He would not stop with Ukraine and our NATO allies would be next."North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible", noting the sanctions legislation passed the chamber with a large, bipartisan majority.Trump could bring down energy prices "by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin," he said.Nebraska Representative Don Bacon said many lawmakers will now resist funding the president's agenda "knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus".The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort.Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter."Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.Negotiators from Ukraine spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and both teams could meet next week, he also said.Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies initially criticised Trump for his plans to import Russian diesel in hopes of bringing down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel. Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Zelensky expressed surprise at the announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days of fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.Trump, condemned Ukraine's strikes as a disgrace, but Zelensky said he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests".

schema.headline: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies

title: North Korea: What satellite images reveal about Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
description: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreatImage source, Vantor/BBCBySoram CheonBBC Korean and Aghnia Adz
body: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreatImage source, Vantor/BBCBySoram CheonBBC Korean and Aghnia AdzkiaEast Asia Visual JournalismAn 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year. What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula. This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size."In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho. Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership.The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures. The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme.Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour, and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished.But the regime has long been known to live in luxury. We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m.While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view.Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule.A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer.North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it.North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors.State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, North Korean tourists on a beach in KalmaA South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227.For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure.Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed.Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays".Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ordinary North Koreans struggle to earn a decent living  The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year.The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July.Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan.Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel.Image source, VantorImage caption, The 50m vessel was seen in waters near Tae island on 4 July 2026.Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view".The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week.Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea.Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told The Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding.He also described a 60m vessel they used as a cross between a ferry and a Disney boat. It is not clear if this is the same 60m boat pictured in the above satellite imagery.To most North Koreans, the life lived by the Kims and others who support the regime would seem not just extravagant but unimaginable. Especially because state propaganda is dedicated to presenting the "supreme leader" as a selfless man who always puts the nation first."Kim Jong Un is supposed to be a 'leader of the people'," Ri Jong Ho says, "yet he has four luxury vessels like these while ordinary people are struggling just to get one meal a day."Graphics by: Arvin Supriyadi

schema.headline: North Korea: What satellite images reveal about Kim Jong Un's summer retreat

title: Florian Wirtz delivers for Liverpool - but is playmaker Andoni Iraola's great conundrum?
description: Figure caption, Liverpool come from behind to beat nine-man BrentfordByHarry PooleBBC Sport journalistFlorian Wirtz was instrumental as Liverpool retu
body: Figure caption, Liverpool come from behind to beat nine-man BrentfordByHarry PooleBBC Sport journalistFlorian Wirtz was instrumental as Liverpool returned to winning ways in the Premier League at Brentford on Saturday, but does the German playmaker remain boss Andoni Iraola's greatest conundrum?Wirtz has come in for criticism amid his struggles to replicate the form which persuaded the Reds to pay Bayer Leverkusen what was a club record £116m in June 2025.Liverpool legend Steven Gerrard even said this week that the 23-year-old could benefit from being taken out of the team altogether, to overcome what the club's former captain perceives as a lack of confidence.The key dilemma facing Iraola was again evident in west London on Saturday.Liverpool bounced back from their first league defeat of the season against Manchester City last weekend by scoring twice in the second half against a Brentford side reduced to 10 men before half-time.The visitors produced plenty of chances, particularly with their man advantage in the second half when they registered 14 of their total 21 attempts.Wirtz was at the heart of things in the final third.The Germany international created more chances from open play (nine) than any other player has managed in a Premier League game over the past six seasons.The last player to create as many chances in a single game in the competition was Sadio Mane, for Liverpool against Burnley, in January 2021 (also nine).In an away game, he is the first player to reach that tally in more than 15 years, since Samir Nasri registered 10 for Manchester City against Tottenham in August 2011.Image caption, Florian Wirtz completed 53 of the 65 passes he attempted (81.5%) - including a match-leading 38 inside the final thirdDespite answering his critics with those standout statistics, the impact of his playing style on the dynamic of the team continues to come under scrutiny.BBC Sport pundit and former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy believes a midfield which features Wirtz as the number 10 remains a problem as it makes Iraola's side too easy to play against."They got the job done. First and foremost, that's another win on the road, which is always positive," Murphy said of Liverpool's performance."But I thought they looked too easy to play against. The spaces are too big. "They're playing with two wingers and Wirtz at 10, so they're relying heavily on the two midfield players to try and cover so much space. "It was too easy for Brentford to play out and to get in behind. That would be the biggest concern today for me."Wirtz's strengths are clear.Following his latest performance, no player has created more chances in the Premier League this season. He is level with Brighton's Pascal Gross on 18.He played in Munoz to begin Liverpool's fightback, meaning Wirtz has assisted in back-to-back games for Liverpool across all competitions for the first time - although this was only his second goal involvement in seven league games this term.He was at the heart of Liverpool's attack, with a match-leading 12 final-third entries and 37 passes in the final third.However, only Milos Kerkez (20) lost possession on more occasions than Wirtz (19) among Liverpool players, and he won just one of his nine duels."They don't look solid and don't look together in terms of shape," Murphy said."Instead of a number 10, where Wirtz is struggling to impact games, put three midfielders in."Always, the priority is foundation, defence, stability, being hard to beat. The other stuff can follow from there. "At the moment, it just looks a little bit open. Against better teams, you're going to get hurt."Figure caption, Liverpool players in 'delicate' situation over 'demanding' schedule - IraolaVictory took Liverpool up to fifth in the table, with three wins from their first seven league games under Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot in the summer.The Spaniard oversaw the Reds' first away league win after conceding first since December 2023, ending a run of 19 winless away games when going 1-0 behind.But, while striker Alexander Isak returned from injury, Iraola was dealt fresh blows as Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong suffered injuries on Saturday.Iraola told BBC Sport: "When you come here, you see the results of Brentford at home and you have to be ready for this kind of battle. "We had a lot of chances. Even at the end, we had some counters where we were three against one and need to finish. When we go 2-1, every throw-in and every free-kick can be a problem."We are in a delicate situation with some of the players. We were talking about this run of four games in 10 days, it's very, very demanding. "We have to rest again because we have another big, big game against Villarreal [in the Champions League on Tuesday]."Figure caption, Liverpool fan delighted with Florian Wirtz's performance at BrentfordFollow Liverpool on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical Reds contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about Liverpool

schema.headline: Florian Wirtz delivers for Liverpool - but is playmaker Andoni Iraola's great conundrum?

title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
description: A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.Belgium condemned the assault on its consul
body: A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look".It was also condemned by the US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".In Saturday's incident the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice."Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said. "As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. "Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters.""According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground."It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged.""The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

schema.headline: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank

title: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says
description: The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.It will be replac
body: The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.It will be replaced by a spin-off show featuring highlights from past episodes. Sources denied reports in the Sun newspaper the programme would be axed as part of a plan to make savings. Presented by Nick Knowles, DIY SOS sees a team transform the homes of families who are facing severe illness, disability, bereavement or building disasters.It was first broadcast in 1999 and is currently airing its 35th series on BBC One and iPlayer.The decision comes during the corporation's drive to save £500m over three years. It has already cancelled several well-known TV shows including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live At The Apollo.A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC's savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore."DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show's past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year."

schema.headline: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says

title: Three takeaways from Elon Musk's latest political donations
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByAna FaguyWashington DCBillionaire Tesla CEO Elon Musk is once again pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into a US elec
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByAna FaguyWashington DCBillionaire Tesla CEO Elon Musk is once again pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into a US election - this time with the aim of helping Republicans maintain their control of Congress.Musk donated upwards of $200m (£150m) in the quarter that ended on 30 September, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings reviewed by the BBC.The fillings were released with just over two weeks until the 2026 midterm election, where many races for the House of Representatives and Senate are close and Republicans risk losing their majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate. Musk also put significant money, $290m, and effort into helping elect President Donald Trump and other Republicans in 2024.Here is where the richest person in the world has been donating this time around, and what it might mean for his businesses. Most of the donations went to one groupThe bulk of the money donated last quarter by the world's only trillionaire, $158m, went to the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) Pac, the filings showed.It is one of the largest publicly known single political donations in US history, and some have suggested it is the biggest ever.SLF is a super Pac backing Republican Senate candidates in tough races.It quickly sent the money on to a group supporting Texas Republican Ken Paxton. The state attorney general, Paxton is at risk of losing to Democrat James Talarico in a race for a seat his party has held for decades. They have been polling neck and neck and the election's outcome is considered a bellwether for the future of Republican power.Super Pacs are independent "political action committees" that can raise unlimited amounts of money and play a major role in funding US political campaigns.Musk also donated more than $80m to the America Pac that he founded during the 2024 election.Texas is a key focus for MuskAmerica Pac last quarter spent millions on digital communications, mailings and phone calls opposing Talarico, as well as thousands on political marketing to support Paxton.At the same time, Musk donated another $10m to Lone Star Liberty Pac, a group primarily backing Paxton, records show.The flow of money highlights a major theme for Musk: Texas.In recent years, the tech CEO has been moving his business empire -  including SpaceX, Tesla and X - to the southern US state after expressing frustration with operating in California.Texas has offered Musk fewer government regulations and no state personal income tax and no corporate income tax.Keeping politicians who favour looser government restrictions in charge, as Republicans typically have, could help maintain that environment for Musk.And his big spending in Texas and in the Texas Senate race seems to point to Musk's understanding of that, political analyst Cayce Myers told the BBC."Republicans have a fundraising advantage this time, but fundraising by itself does not actually guarantee success," he said.A broader trend for tech executivesFor many voters this year, technology has become a top issue. People across the country are pushing for increased government oversight of artificial intelligence,  data centres and social media.That's something that has tech leaders like Musk developing closer ties to the Republican party, which historically has promoted lighter government regulation, Myers said."What [tech leaders] are looking at is a future where there is growing demand and call for regulation and I think they want to be in an advantageous position," he said. "We're seeing them shift, and fall behind Republicans."Other tech leaders, such as OpenAI president and his wife Greg and Anna Brockman are also putting big money behind Republicans.The couple donated $25m to the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc Pac last year.Myer noted it's not just the tech sector, but industries like cryptocurrency and gambling where large sums of money are being donated in an attempt to exert influence."This is the idea of shaping the regulatory environment through contributions," he said.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Three takeaways from Elon Musk's latest political donations

title: France protests: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as over 1,000 arrested
description: Figure caption, How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across FranceByJack BurgessViolence broke out across France on Saturday during the
body: Figure caption, How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across FranceByJack BurgessViolence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living.At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds. Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported.Figure caption, Watch: Moment historic French town hall spire collapses in flames amid protestsPrime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest.In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République.Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fireIn Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse.A young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened."The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied.Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers.Image source, ReutersImage caption, A car was set alight at the Place de la République in ParisHundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups. These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty.French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party.The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Rapid-response riot police were deployed in Paris Prime Minister Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical".He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence."Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence.French President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October.However, the protests have continued and intensified.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Shops were looted in Paris, and other cities, during demonstrations on Saturday

schema.headline: France protests: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as over 1,000 arrested

title: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year
description: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.The 22-year-old Londoner is a prof
body: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral."The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says.The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first.He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms.The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible.For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping.He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests.Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says.Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says.Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world".Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick.The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max.For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs.That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos.In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips."The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions".

schema.headline: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year
